https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgj.text: Image source, Reuters By Brandon Drenon and Kennedy Gotham Published 11 August 2026, 16:35 BST Updated 1 hour ago President Donald Trump said a US Marine held in a Russian prison, whose health was reportedly in extremely poor condition, has been released. "After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that no prisoner swap took place. In 2022, Gilman, who is from Massachusetts, was arrested for allegedly kicking a police officer while aboard a train. He had recently been moved from prison to a civilian hospital in Russia after going into a catatonic-like state. Trump said the 32-year-old was on a flight back to the US accompanied by his mother, doctors, and members of the administration. According to a statement from his family, Gilman is expected to later arrive at a US military hospital in Texas where he will be assessed and treated. His health was in "life-threatening condition" after he was subjected to "harsh and abusive treatment", the family said. "The Russians treated my brother so badly. They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both and American and a Marine," his sister, Lexi Hudson, said in the statement. "I am so grateful to President Trump for saving my brother's life," she added. Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey also helped secure her brother's release, she said. In a statement, Markey said: "Approximately 50 days ago, Robert was diagnosed with a dissociative stupor - a condition where he is non-responsive and unable to interact or eat. " In Russian confinement, Gilman was subject to repeated harassment, including forced exercise training sessions that lasted up to 16 hours and the administration of psychotropic drugs, Eric Lebson, who advocated for Gilman's release as part of the group Global Reach, told CBS News, the BBC's media partner. The abuse was so severe that at one point Gilman had required a feeding tube in his nose, according to Lebson. Gilman served in the US Marines from August 2019 to August 2020. He was arrested for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk aboard a train to Moscow in January 2022 and was initially given a sentence of three and a half years. He was later found guilty of assaulting prison guards, after he allegedly attacked a prison inspector during a cell check. His sentence was then increased to 10 years. Lebson said five other Americans remain in Russia, each contending with medical issues. Their names are Aleksandr Antonov, David Barnes, Olga Jezler, Andre Khachatoorian, and Chuck Zimmerman. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cy4k1j.text: Watch: What is it like to travel on Air Force One with Trump? Watch: What is it like to travel on Air Force One with Trump? Close President Donald Trump secretly swapped planes as he left a Nato summit in Turkey last month, according to US media. Footage from 8 July shows him boarding Air Force One, the presidential jet, at Ankara airport. But according to the Washington Post, he was then secretly taken to a smaller C-32A military aircraft - a modified Boeing 757 often used by the vice-president - via a catering truck, which had been elevated to plane level on the opposite side to where he had boarded. Journalists and some White House staff boarded Air Force One and were reportedly told to close their window shades. They were unaware the president was no longer on board. The BBC's State Department correspondent Tom Bateman shares what it's like to be onboard Air Force One with the president as part of the press pool. Read more about the story here . https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/article.text: Return to Homepage Top Stories: Tropical Storm Lala tracker Virginia State University shooting Gen Z loves sports betting Looming Social Security crisis USS Lincoln concerns Luigi Mangione pleads guilty Trump admin departures Big Bend bulldozing Hello Kitty x Godzilla Powerball jackpot winner Latvia organised together with NATO in 2025 anti-drone military exercises that featured some home-grown tech (Gints Ivuskans) When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Rapolas Markevicius was managing a private equity fund in Lithuania -- a country on NATO's eastern flank that fears it might be Moscow's next target. Four and a half years later, his new startup Pdkinematics builds precision guidance systems that help drones strike targets more accurately even when GPS signals are jammed, which are supplied to both Ukraine and its European allies. He is one of several startup founders in the Baltics trying to invigorate the region's defensive capabilities, as NATO's eastern members face their own hybrid threats from Russia and its close ally Belarus. Advertisement Advertisement "The beginning of the war was kind of a call for action for us," Markevicius told AFP. After Russia's February 2022 invasion, he launched a research and development programme to "understand what kind of technologies we could actually deliver to the battlefront", working with his co-founder from the space-tech sector. As states across NATO's eastern flank face a raft of hostile actions from Moscow and Minsk ranging from drone incursions to cyberattacks, experts say startups like his are improving the region's economic resilience and helping to deter Russian aggression. - 'Scalable solutions' - An active startup scene has developed in Lithuania and its fellow Baltic states of Estonia and Latvia in the decades since their transition from Soviet-controlled command economies. Advertisement Advertisement It is even home to several companies that are now well known far from the Baltics, such as Vinted, Bolt and Skype. Entrepreneurs are filling gaps left by traditional arms contractors. The conflict in Ukraine has seen a massive technological shift in warfare, with drones and robots taking on much of the fighting. That has put a premium on quick development as well as the capacity to rapidly scale up production. "The current technology that will drive, and is currently driving, the transition of European arms must be as scalable as it must be high-tech," Markevicius said. And, he added, it is usually startups that are "creating quite efficient, cost-efficient and scalable solutions". Advertisement Advertisement - 'Tried and tested' - The Baltic states have some of the highest defence spending in all of NATO in relative terms -- Lithuania directs 5.3 percent of GDP to defence, the most of NATO's 32 members. Governments are more open to working with less experienced contractors given the speed at which warfare is transforming. The Lithuanian Armed Forces provide access to fields and airspace every month as a practical testing grounds for emerging technologies. The Ukraine war is also giving companies real-time feedback on how their technologies fare against the Russian military. "You can test your product with Ukraine, with Lithuanian soldiers, with any NATO soldiers," said Elvinas Kukys, CEO and founder of Luna Robotics, a startup developing advanced imaging systems for FPV drones. Advertisement Advertisement In that environment, defence startups across the region have been able to attract significant foreign investment. "The Baltic states have really been tried and tested over the past four years about how they needed to restructure their economies, reorient and really invest in their defence capabilities," said Mario Bikarski, Senior Europe Analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. "They are really now some of the best-prepared countries to withstand a wide range of new forms of attacks," he added. - 'A new normal' - A burgeoning defence startup sector "is not something that is going to stop a potential Russian attack", Milan Trajkovic, an analyst at Fitch, told AFP. Advertisement Advertisement "But it does probably make it more difficult," he added. Invest Lithuania (IL), which helps foreign firms invest in the country, said the Baltics' position next to Russia means some investors require reassurance. "We understand that this is the new normal," said its general manager Elijus Civilis. He said meetings between investors and government ministries -- sometimes involving confidential information -- can help calm some fears and promote a better image of the country and region. "We have many international troops, we have armour, we have vehicles, we have everything we haven't had before," he said. ks/jc/rl/yad/rmb/lga Advertisement About Our Ads About Our Ads Recommended articles 5 people injured in shooting at Virginia State University Five people were injured in the shooting involving multiple suspects. https://www.dw.com/en/croatia-monster-fi.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MWfY The fire spread through remote parts of the island before threatening populated coastal areas Image: Ivo Cagalj/Pixsell/IMAGO Advertisement Nearly 700 people were evacuated amid a wildfire on the Adriatic island of Brac, Croatian media outlets reported on Sunday, following a tense night which saw hundreds of firefighters defending homes and tourist accommodations from the approaching blaze. The situation was especially dramatic near the small town of Milna on the island's western coast. "Last night was a disaster. It was simply impossible," Milna Mayor Frane Lozic told Net.hr news outlet. "I would have not believed that [the fire] can wipe out everything in its path so quickly." Over 220 firefighters and 69 vehicles fought the blaze overnight Image: Ivo Cagalj/Pixsell/IMAGO The fire was first reported on Thursday, but firefighting efforts were complicated by inaccessible terrain. Even so, Lozic said that the authorities believed they had the situation in hand by Saturday. "We thought we got it reined in yesterday, that it is all over, and then it happened: Sea wind starts blowing at 9 p.m. and out of nowhere, there is a monster," he said. No deaths reported in blaze Tourist ships joined the rescue efforts overnight, with many tourists spending the night at the beach, waiting to be evacuated. No deaths were reported due to the blaze. However, one 76-year-old Croatian woman was hospitalized in critical condition, according to Index.hr news portal. The woman is believed to have fallen off a ship during the evacuation process. A 27-year-old man required medical aid for smoke inhalation and was then released. Authorities estimated some 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) were affected by the fire, according to a report by the AFP news agency. Officials confirmed some buildings were damaged, but said it was too early for a full damage assessment. Firefighting planes active on the scene As of Sunday morning, Croatian authorities said there were no more "open fires" but added teams were still in the field to prevent reignition. Four specialized firefighting planes are also operating in the area. The blaze on the island of Brac was visible from Croatia's second city, Split Image: Zvonimir Barisin/Pixsell/IMAGO Two government ministers and the head of Croatia's national firefighting service are set to attend a high-level meeting on Brac this afternoon with local officials and leaders of the local firefighting teams, after which they are expected to provide more information about the blaze. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Abhijeet Dipke's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has drawn thousands onto the streets in recent months By Zoya Mateen, Azadeh Moshiri & Vikas Pandey BBC News, Delhi Published 16 October 2026, 00:30 BST Updated 8 hours ago Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of India's "cockroach" movement, and a few others were detained in Delhi as police tried to stop a protest demanding the resignation of the country's election chief. Hundreds had gathered in Connaught Place, one of the capital's busiest commercial districts, waving Indian flags and shouting slogans despite a heavy security presence. Police sealed off Central Park, the planned site of the protest, and deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel to prevent the gathering. The Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) accuses India's Election Commission of manipulating voter lists to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling BJP. Both deny the allegation. The group has held a series of protests in Delhi in recent weeks, with police repeatedly detaining its leaders and supporters. Friday's demonstration unfolded under similarly heavy security presence, though the police response was more restrained than during last weekend's sweeping crackdown. Hours before the protest, police went to the house where Dipke was staying. In an exchange broadcast live on Instagram, he challenged officers who had come to caution him against holding the march, asking whether waving the Indian flag was against the law. Hours later, the BBC saw officers surround Dipke as he approached his car and force him into a police vehicle. Some supporters tried to stop it from leaving. It was Dipke's second detention in less than a week. Last Saturday, police had boarded his plane shortly after it landed in Delhi to prevent him from reaching another demonstration. He was released the following day. The movement's two other main leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were also detained last weekend and later released. But on Wednesday, they were sent to jail for five days after returning to Jantar Mantar, a protest site near parliament that police had recently declared off-limits. Friday's march was partly intended to demand the release of Das and Ranka. Dipke's detention means the movement's three main leaders are once again in custody. The CJP said it had lost contact with him and accused police of taking him to an undisclosed location and denying him access to lawyers. But they insist the arrests and detentions will not stop them. "They may detain three people, but how will they stop 30 tomorrow? How will they stop 300 leaders?" CJP spokesperson Mehr Pasricha told the BBC. Police have not publicly confirmed the grounds for Dipke's detention or responded to the CJP's latest allegations. Anish Gawande, the opposition politician who had been hosting Dipke, also questioned the police action. "Detaining a lone man walking with the national flag in his hand is a bit of a joke," he said. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Hundreds of people gathered in central Delhi to unfurl the national flag as part of the protest At Connaught Place, the police presence dwarfed the protest itself. Around 200-300 people initially gathered outside Central Park, which authorities had closed. Unable to enter, they walked around its perimeter, waving Indian flags and shouting slogans. More protesters arrived as the evening progressed. Officers kept emerging from buses parked around the district. Journalists crowded the streets too, and together with police, they far outnumbered the demonstrators. For much of the evening, police largely held back, with the BBC witnessing only a handful of detentions. But as darkness fell, officers began using force against some protesters. The BBC saw some young demonstrators being pushed into a bus where women were already being held. Inside were around 50 female officers, far more than the number of detainees. The BBC also saw two people being injured during the police action. One protester fell to the ground and appeared to have hurt their leg. Among those detained was Neha Bora , a prominent leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) who has emerged as one of the faces of the recent protests. She had also been detained during last weekend's crackdown. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Student activist Neha Bora is among the people detained by the Delhi police on Friday evening Barely five months old, the CJP began as an online campaign in May after India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches. Dipke embraced the insult and turned it into a rallying cry. By July, the group had become a formidable force, drawing thousands of young people into protests over leaked exam papers. A march towards parliament in July descended into clashes with police, bringing the movement wider attention and intensifying pressure on the government. The unrest eventually forced the resignation of India's education minister. The CJP has since turned its attention to India's electoral system, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a sweeping revision of voter lists known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). Critics say the exercise risks removing legitimate voters from the rolls, potentially depriving them of the right to vote. The Election Commission says it is targeting ineligible, dead and duplicate voters and denies allegations that it is favouring the ruling BJP. Last weekend, authorities imposed severe restrictions to stop CJP supporters from reaching a planned rally, sealing off roads, shutting metro stations and deploying thousands of security personnel across Delhi. The BBC witnessed , external dozens of protesters being detained across the capital, including students and journalists. The action drew criticism but police defended it as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings. Dipke, Das and Ranka were released the following day after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour. But the dispute over where they could protest was only beginning. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Delhi authorities have said Central Park is closed on Friday and Saturday for "administrative reasons" Police removed Jantar Mantar from Delhi's list of approved protest sites, naming three alternative venues. Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory stands close to Parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent. The CJP accused authorities of trying to push demonstrations away from the seat of power. On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned to the restricted site with a handful of supporters, unfurling the Indian flag and shouting slogans against Kumar. Police said some protesters had climbed over a locked gate and that the organisers had breached the conditions of their release. The following day, the two men were sent to jail for five days. The arrests did little to deter the movement from announcing another demonstration. In a video message on Thursday, Dipke urged supporters unable to travel to Delhi to raise the Indian flag in their own towns and cities. He also acknowledged the possibility of being arrested again. "I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said. By Friday morning, police had served him with a notice warning against holding the march without permission. Authorities closed Central Park for two days, citing "administrative reasons", and offered to let a small group wave the national flag and sing the anthem at another location. The CJP came up with a different plan. Supporters were told to enter Connaught Place in groups of fewer than five, unfurl the flag, take a photograph and leave. "Waving the Tiranga is not a crime," the movement declared in a social media poster, using the Hindi name for India's tricolour. It urged supporters to share their photographs online. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Sporadic protests erupted around the Central Park on Friday evening despite the detentions Opposition parties have also been holding protests against Kumar and the Election Commission. Last week, Rahul Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were detained while attempting to march to the commission's headquarters. They have also taken their concerns to President Droupadi Murmu and marched towards the Supreme Court. Gandhi has condemned the arrests of CJP leaders and called for Jantar Mantar to be reopened to protesters, although the opposition and the youth-led movement have largely demonstrated separately. Home Minister Amit Shah has accused the opposition of spreading falsehoods about the voter-list revision and defended the commission's independence. For the CJP, the immediate question is how long it can sustain its protests with its three main leaders in custody. Pasricha said the party had a team and a plan in place. "If the top three continue to stay behind bars, we will continue to protest peacefully," she said.
